job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up for dawn prayer, then I go for a walk before the city wakes up. At eight I'm at my desk, a plank on two crates in the room I rent in Millbrook with a flatmate called Kofi. I spend the morning on two things: applications and my side project, an inventory app for corner shops that my friend Idris and I are building. In the afternoon I visit shops to test it, and in the evening I work a few hours on a food-delivery bike, which pays the room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and how's the job search?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer engineering, finished in June with a good result. My final project was a barcode stock scanner, and I did ten weeks at a logistics software company, writing test scripts. Then the firm said the budget was cut. I've sent over a hundred applications, had four interviews and no offers. I'm carrying heavy student debt, I have under a month of costs saved if I live on rice, and my family back home can't help, they're stretched. So the delivery bike is how I eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always going to be a bit of both, some useful tools and a lot of noise. I'd tell the guys at the mosque that hard work and good habits still beat any technology. I'd also say the real shortage is of employers willing to give young people a chance, and it's up to us to create our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the job market stays poor for beginners, and that's what I have to live with. With a hundred applications and four interviews, I know it's not about being good enough, it's about being noticed. I don't blame AI. I blame a market where five hundred people chase every graduate role. Still, I'm anxious, because the loan won't wait for the market to get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the shop app harder. We have two shops testing it, and I'd try to get ten paying at fifteen pounds a month. I'd keep riding the bike in the evenings and save what I can. I'd also keep applying to jobs, in case the app doesn't pay, but I'd tell employers about the app, because it shows I can build and sell something. And I'd use AI to speed up our code and our sales emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless but driven. A bit like waiting for a bus, except I'm also building a bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the shop app going, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It works, but it's slow. Two shops use it every day. One owner, Mr Patel, says it saved him an hour a day on counting stock. That's the proof. But getting shops to pay is harder than building the code, because they've been doing it on paper for twenty years and they don't trust new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think a young person should expect from an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they should get what they earn. I believe in work and in fair pay for it, and I don't love when people say the state owes them. But I do think firms should give a fair shot to a young person and pay for what they do. And I'd say, if no one will hire you, create something. That's what I'm trying.

say: I'd tell the men at the mosque that hard work and good habits still beat any **technology**.
The real shortage is employers willing to give young people a chance.
think: The market is poor for beginners, and the problem is being **noticed**, not being good enough.
The loan won't wait for the market to get better.
do: Push the shop app and aim for ten **paying** shops at fifteen pounds a month.
Keep riding the delivery bike in the evenings and save what I can.
Keep applying to jobs and mention the app, which shows I can build and sell.
feel: **Restless** but driven, like building a bike while waiting for a bus.
Anxious because the loan won't wait.
S0.quote: Getting shops to pay is harder than building the code, because they've been doing it on paper for twenty years and they don't trust new things.
fieldNote: He is **entrepreneurial**: his answer to a closed market is to build and sell something.
Mr Patel's saved hour is proof he can cite, which helps his **pitch**.
Free-market views show in his language of earning, fair pay and a fair **shot**.

steps.text: Sign ten corner shops at fifteen pounds a month
Keep riding the delivery bike on weekday evenings
Use AI to write sales emails and speed up the app code
Keep applying for software jobs and mention the shop app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people who can adapt will win. I'd say to my flatmate and the guys at the mosque, learn the tools, offer a service, don't wait for a boss to tell you what to do. I'd also say the market will sort it out if we let people try things, but we should help people who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a big shake-up for graduates like me, but I think I'm better placed than most. The test scripts I wrote at the logistics firm, AI now writes. That's the entry-level job gone. But shops like Mr Patel's need someone who can set up and explain tools to people who aren't technical, and that's me. The risk is that firms hire fewer people and I'm still at the bottom of the pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change the shop app into a package: the app, a short setup visit and a monthly check-in. I'd add an AI feature that predicts what to reorder and price that higher. I'd study how AI agents work, using free courses, and I'd offer to build tools for other small businesses. And I'd keep applying to jobs, for money security, in case I need a steady pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. It's like surfing, I think. If you stay on the board it's great, and if you fall it's cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks does AI already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own coding, a good deal of it. I use an AI assistant every day and I reckon it writes half my code now. Test scripts, small functions, even documentation. The bits that are left are knowing what to build and checking that it's right. That's what I need to be best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's most at risk among the people you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the people who keep the books and do the ordering in small offices, and the friends of mine in call centres. They're the first in the firing line. Their jobs are the card's list: answering customers, booking, checking. They don't have an app on the side, and I worry for them.

say: I'd tell my flatmate and friends to learn the tools, **offer** a service and not wait for a boss.
The market will sort it out if we let people try things.
think: The test scripts I wrote at the logistics firm are now written by AI, so the entry-level job is **gone**.
Shops need someone who can set up and explain tools to non-technical people.
do: Turn the shop app into a **package**: app, setup visit and monthly check-in.
Add an AI reorder-prediction feature and price it higher.
Study AI agents through free courses and keep applying for steady jobs.
feel: Great if you stay on the board, cold if you fall.
S1.quote: The bits that are left are knowing what to build and checking that it's right. That's what I need to be best at.
fieldNote: He admits AI writes **half** his code, and sees what remains as judgement.
He worries openly about call-centre and bookkeeping friends, which shows **concern** beyond himself.
He has a business answer in mind but keeps **job applications** open for security.

steps.text: Package the shop app with a setup visit and monthly check-in
Add an AI reorder-prediction feature and charge more for it
Study AI agents through free online courses
Keep applying for steady jobs for security

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test, for governments and for us. I'd say that people with skills should help others, and the community should look after those who fall behind. I'd also say, honestly, that we should ask what's the point of the technology if it only makes a few people rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm deeply afraid. Two years is not enough time. My field is the first to go, and my app is just a small product that an AI agent could build in an afternoon. I'd still have the loan, a few small customers, and no room to grow. I think it could break me if I let it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for survival. I'd use every hour on the bike and any odd job, save every pound and cut the room cost by moving into a shared place with more people. I'd ask the mosque and my family if they can help, even if it's hard to ask. I'd also look at jobs that need people in person, care, repair and logistics, where robots come later. And I'd keep the app running as a small side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. It's a coldness I know from when I first left home. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your faith tell you to do when something like this arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably sell it or give it away. If an AI can build a stock app in an afternoon, nobody pays fifteen pounds a month for mine. Maybe I'd keep the shop relationships, because trust is something the machine doesn't have. The shop owner Mr Patel doesn't pay for software, he pays for me turning up and fixing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the shop app in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My faith tells me to be patient and to help others. In a hard time, I'd share what I have and I'd lean on what my community gives. It also tells me not to put my trust in a machine or a salary. That's strange comfort, but it's real.

say: I'd say it's a test for governments and for us, and the community should look after those who fall **behind**.
The technology has no point if it only makes a few people rich.
think: Two years is not enough, and my app is a small product an AI agent could build in an **afternoon**.
I'd still have the loan and no room to grow.
do: Use every hour on the **bike** and any odd job, and move to a cheaper shared place.
Ask the mosque and my family for help, even if it's hard to ask.
Look at in-person work like care, repair and logistics.
feel: **Shaken**, with a coldness I remember from first leaving home.
I'd pray more and sleep less.
S2.quote: The shop owner Mr Patel doesn't pay for software, he pays for me turning up and fixing it.
fieldNote: His **business** instinct holds: trust and presence are what a machine lacks.
Faith gives him a **frame**, patience and sharing, rather than a plan.
He knows his product is easy to copy, and says it **plainly**.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper shared room
Ask the mosque and my family for help
Look for in-person repair and logistics jobs
Keep the shop app running as small side income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something, so let's be builders. I'd tell the lads at the mosque and in the flat to get a skill that serves people directly, and to save. I'd say don't wait for a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a fight I think I can have. I'd have time to grow the shops, maybe earn enough to hire someone, and learn what's next. Because the tools change quickly, I'd have to keep learning every month. If I stay ahead of the tools, I think I can stay useful past the date. It's not certain, but it's not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign more shops and push the app toward a service: stock, ordering, and an AI assistant that talks to suppliers. I'd save at least a third of everything and pay off the highest-interest part of the loan. I'd also take a short course in cybersecurity or data protection, since small firms need to trust whoever handles their data. And I'd get a steady day job if one came along, to fund the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, alert. A bit like the start of Ramadan, where you know it's going to be hard but you know how to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year with five years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but with care. I'd focus on the shops that value the service and not the cheapest software. I'd grow slowly with maybe thirty shops, then add suppliers. If AGI arrives in 2031, a business with human relationships and local trust might survive longer than a pure software company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try to grow the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year is about proving the shops will pay and the loan can be managed. I'd keep the bike for six months to build a cushion, then drop it once the app pays the rent. That's the plan, and I've told Idris, so now he can hold me to it.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **build** something, so let's be builders.
think: It's a fight I think I can have: time to grow the shops and keep **learning** every month.
If I stay ahead of the tools, I can stay useful past the date.
do: Sign more shops and push the app toward a **service** with an AI supplier assistant.
Save a third of everything and pay off the highest-interest loan part.
Take a short data protection course and keep the bike for six months.
feel: Like the start of Ramadan, hard but I know how to do it.
S3.quote: A business with human relationships and local trust might survive longer than a pure software company.
fieldNote: Five years lets him think about **relationships**, not just code.
He wants to sell **trust** with data protection, which small firms need.
Idris, his business partner, holds him to the plan, and he finds that **useful**.

steps.text: Sign thirty corner shops and add a supplier-ordering service
Save a third of income and pay the highest-interest loan first
Take a short data protection course
Keep the delivery bike for six months for a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and what we do with it is up to us. I'd say start small, build slowly, and share what you know. I'd also say employers should offer paid training, because they'll need loyal people in ten years' time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm, but I won't be careless. Ten years lets me build a real firm, maybe five or six employees, learn from my mistakes, and still have time to change. The change will happen, and by then I'd have a track record, savings and people who trust me. That's a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the business first, then expand to services that need people on the ground, like setting up shops with robots and AI that arrive later. I'd pay off the loan in four or five years, get married, perhaps, and send money to my parents. I'd keep learning every year, and put a share of profit into a small trust fund for my family's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, even optimistic. It feels like the first real chance I've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you stay in the same business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, though I'd change what it sells. The version I have now is small. In ten years I'd want to run something that helps small shops adopt robots and AI, installing and servicing them. If shops need help moving to automation, someone has to walk in and do it, and that can be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at 33?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, with a small home, running a firm with a few employees and helping my parents. I'd have my loan paid off. I'd want to be someone who made jobs, not just took one. That's the best part of this: with ten years, I could be the one who hires the next graduate.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and what we do with it is up to us.
think: I'm calm but not careless: ten years lets me build a real firm with a **track record**.
The change will happen, but I'd have savings and people who trust me.
do: Build the business first, then expand to **services** that put robots and AI into shops.
Pay off the loan in four or five years and send money to my parents.
Keep learning every year and put a share of profit into a family fund.
feel: The first real chance I've had.
S4.quote: I'd want to be someone who made jobs, not just took one.
fieldNote: With ten years he moves from survival to **ambition**: a firm that installs and services automation.
His hope to **hire** the next graduate is a clear contrast to his own search.
He still carries the loan and a family back home, which keep him uneasy.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan within five years
Grow the firm to five or six employees
Add installation and servicing of AI and robots for small shops
Send money home to my parents each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is not enough to build anything that lasts, and the product I'm making is the kind of thing an AI could make quickly. What would help is practical: loan payments that wait until I'm earning, small-business support that doesn't take a year to arrive, and an honest sense from firms of what skills they actually want. And decent first jobs for graduates, not unpaid internships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't want to be seen as a victim. I'm trying to build my own way, and I'll keep doing it. But I'd like people to know that for a lot of us graduates, the bike and the app and the applications are happening all at once, and nobody's holding a safety net. I'd like fewer lectures and more openings.

headlineQuote: For a lot of us graduates, the bike and the app and the applications are happening all at once, and nobody's holding a safety net.
portrait: Umar is a **23-year-old** computer engineering graduate in a rented room, with over a hundred applications, four interviews and no offer.
He rides a delivery bike to eat and builds a **stock app** for corner shops with his friend Idris.
He leans traditional and free-market, values faith and community, and prefers building his own work to waiting for handouts.
Adaptive and risk-tolerant, he uses AI daily and reframes his business around **trust**, service and local relationships.
He is anxious in most pictures, alarmed with two years, and uneasy with ten, when he imagines hiring others.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most, because two years is too short and his product is easy for AI to copy.
whatWouldHelp: Loan payments that **wait** until he's earning, quick small-business support, and decent paid first jobs for graduates.
